passage: I'm Disha, Mehak's roommate. She asked me to sit two tables away at the tea shop near Sector 17, 'just in case'. Her father arrived early, holding a box of pinnis, which she used to love. They didn't hug. He said something and she nodded; later she told me they'd agreed not to talk about the fight today. For forty minutes they discussed her exams, his new scooter, the rain. Near the end she said something slowly, looking at her cup. He looked up, and his eyes were wet. He answered. When they left, he paid, and she let him. She told me afterwards she'd said, 'I missed you,' and he'd said, 'I was wrong to shout.' They still disagree about most things, she said. But they're meeting again next month.

qa.q: What was Mehak's father holding when he arrived?
qa.a: He was holding a box of pinnis.

qa.q: What might Mehak's father have felt when she spoke into her cup, judging by his wet eyes?
qa.a: He seems moved and relieved to hear 'I missed you', perhaps after months of fearing she didn't.

qa.q: Why was agreeing not to talk about the fight a wise rule for this first meeting?
qa.a: It kept the meeting short and safe, so each could say one true thing without the old argument taking over; harder topics can wait.

qa.q: How does Disha see the meeting from two tables away?
qa.a: She watches carefully without knowing their feelings for sure, noticing cues like the pinnis, the wet eyes and Mehak letting him pay 🙂.

grounding: A roommate watches a young woman and her father meet for tea, set the past aside for the day and each say one true thing.

Tuesday. Vikas typed and deleted the message four times before sending it: 'Tea on Saturday? Just an hour. Can we not talk about last year yet?' Sunaina replied within a minute: 'Yes. Just tea.'
Saturday. At the café near the bus depot, they both ordered masala chai and stirred too long. They talked about his internship, her new job, the neighbour's noisy dog. Before leaving, Vikas said, 'I'm proud of the work I'm doing, Ma. I wanted you to know.' Sunaina said, 'I've kept your room the same. I don't know if that's good or bad.' Neither pushed further.
Wednesday. A photo arrived on Vikas's phone: two cups of chai on her kitchen table. 'Next Saturday?' He wrote back, 'Yes.' Then, a minute later: 'Still don't agree with you about everything.' 'I know,' she replied. 'Come anyway.'

qa.q: How many times did Vikas type and delete the message before sending it?
qa.a: He typed and deleted it four times before sending it.

qa.q: What did Sunaina mean by saying she doesn't know if keeping his room the same is good or bad?
qa.a: She seems unsure whether it shows love or an inability to let go, and she chose to share that uncertain, true feeling rather than a neat one.

qa.q: Which choices made this reunion work in small steps?
qa.a: A one-hour limit, leaving last year for later, each saying one true thing, and agreeing to meet again without needing full agreement.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel when Sunaina replies 'Come anyway'?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and welcomed, seeing that his mother wants him to visit even though they still disagree.

grounding: Over a week a young man and his mother meet for a short tea, avoid the past, share one true thing each, and grow closer without full agreement.

passage:
Come, Vaibhav, sit. You're angry with your brother, I know. Let me tell you about my father.
When I, Irawati, was twenty, I married your Aajoba against Baba's wishes, and Baba did not speak to his only daughter for two years. Then one day he sent word through my aunt: tea, at the station canteen, Sunday.
I almost didn't go. When I sat down, he said, "Let us not open old files today." So we didn't. He told me one true thing: "I missed your laugh." I told him one: "I missed your stories." Then we drank our tea.
We never agreed about my marriage, beta. Not once. But we had tea every month after that until he died. Small steps, Vaibhav.

qa.q: Where did Irawati and her father meet for tea?
qa.a: At the station canteen, on Sunday.

qa.q: What might young Irawati have been feeling when she almost didn't go?
qa.a: She was likely nervous and hurt after two years of silence, afraid the meeting would reopen the fight.

qa.q: In the story, what choice at the tea made the reunion possible?
qa.a: Agreeing not to open old files that day and each saying one true thing, so they could start small.

qa.q: How might Irawati's father have felt saying "I missed your laugh"?
qa.a: He was probably vulnerable and relieved, finally letting his daughter see that he had missed her.

grounding: Shows an elder's story of meeting her estranged father for tea, agreeing not to reargue the past and each saying one true thing.

Chinmay's train left at 6:40, which gave them forty minutes at the station café. Rain drummed on the tin roof. Payal arrived soaked, and for a moment neither of them knew whether to hug.
"Papa."
"Payal."
They ordered two teas. Payal took a breath. "Can we not talk about the course today? Or last year?"
Chinmay nodded. "Today, just tea."
She said, "I've missed you. That's true even though I'm still angry."
He turned his cup. "I was wrong to say you'd fail. I don't agree with your choice. But I was wrong to say that."
The announcer called his train. He stood, then touched her wet hair, once.

qa.q: How long did Payal and Chinmay have at the station café?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she said she'd missed him?
qa.a: She felt torn, missing her father and still angry, and chose to say both honestly.

qa.q: Why did agreeing "Today, just tea" help at this stage?
qa.a: It kept the first meeting small and safe, so old fights did not swallow it.

qa.q: What might Chinmay be experiencing as he touches her wet hair?
qa.a: He may feel tender and regretful, glad to see her even though he still disagrees with her choice.

grounding: Shows a first short meeting for tea where father and daughter agree not to reargue the past and each says one true thing.

passage:
The café near Gariahat was Devika's choice: neutral, noisy, not home. Anjali got there ten minutes early and ordered nothing.
When her mother walked in, she looked smaller than Anjali remembered.
"I thought we could just... have tea," Devika said. "Not go over everything."
"Yes. Please."
They talked about the neighbour's dog, the new flyover, Anjali's hostel food. Then Devika put her cup down. "One true thing. I still think you rushed. But I've hated every day of not talking."
Anjali swallowed. "One true thing back. I'm not sorry I left. I am sorry it's been so long."
They split a plate of fish fry. It wasn't agreement. It was a start.

qa.q: What did Anjali and Devika split?
qa.a: A plate of fish fry.

qa.q: What does Devika looking smaller suggest about how Anjali felt?
qa.a: Anjali seems surprised and moved, perhaps sad at how the time apart has touched her mother.

qa.q: Which choice made this first meeting work?
qa.a: Agreeing not to go over everything and each saying one true thing, even when they still disagree.

qa.q: What is it like for Devika to admit she hated every day of not talking?
qa.a: It is probably hard and exposing for her, but also a relief to say it while keeping her own view.

grounding: Shows a mother and daughter meeting for tea, not reopening old fights, each saying one true thing without full agreement.

"You came," Mridul said, standing up too fast at the corner table.
"I said I would." Sunaina sat. The tea arrived. Neither touched it.
"Before anything," she said, "can we agree not to fight about the past today? Just today."
Her father nodded. "Just tea."
Silence. Somewhere a waiter dropped a spoon.
"Can I say one true thing?" Sunaina asked.
"Please."
"I missed you on my birthday. I kept looking at the phone."
Mridul's eyes filled. "I wrote you a message that day. I didn't send it." He took a breath. "My true thing: I'm proud of your job. I tell people at the office."
Sunaina laughed shakily. "You never told me."
"I'm telling you now."
They didn't agree on anything else. But when they stood, he asked, "Next Sunday? Same table?"
"Same table," she said.

qa.q: What did Mridul do on Sunaina's birthday?
qa.a: He wrote her a message that day but didn't send it.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling as she asked to say one true thing?
qa.a: She was nervous but hopeful, wanting to share honestly that she had missed him without reopening old fights.

qa.q: Why did agreeing not to fight about the past help this meeting?
qa.a: It kept the first meeting small and safe, so each could say one true, tender thing instead of reopening old wounds.

qa.q: How does Mridul experience the meeting?
qa.a: Mridul seems anxious at first, standing too fast, then moved to tears and relieved enough to ask for next Sunday.

grounding: Shows an estranged daughter and father meeting for tea, agreeing not to reopen the past and each saying one true thing, finding closeness without full agreement.
